title: Pulisic double leads US to 6-0 rout of Haiti in Pochettino’s farewell tour
author: Jeff Rueter
text:
US take 5-0 lead in Nations League quarter-final

Hall, 18, scores again as Pochettino prepares for exit

Pulisic goes into fourth on all-time US scoring list

When Mauricio Pochettino named his US roster for the November window, few could have expected that the games would double as his brief lame-duck era. A week of camp instead brought constant media coverage, efficient negotiations and questions about the future of the national team. Come Wednesday, his day job will take him far from the federation’s headquarters in Fayetteville, Georgia, as he hopes to make sense of Manchester United .

Saturday finally allowed Pochettino and his players to get on with the intended purpose of this window, and they took to the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals with aplomb. The US opened their two-leg series against Haiti with a dominant 6-0 victory in front of a considerably pro-Haitian crowd in Miami. Auston Trusty provided the first half’s only goal before Julian Hall, Christian Pulisic , Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun contributed to the eventual rout.

Concacaf allowed Haiti to host the match in Miami under an “exceptional hosting arrangement” because of the ongoing political unrest and gang violence in Port-au-Prince.

Pochettino’s penultimate lineup as US manager built on the momentum fostered during the previous international window. Tyler Adams retained the captain’s armband after being named permanent skipper in September, a decision on which Pochettino’s successor would be foolish to renege.

Trusty partnered Chris Richards between the first-choice full-back tandem of Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman. Pulisic and McKennie made their first international appearances since the World Cup. Diego Kochen and Hall started in goal and at striker, respectively, as two members of a rising generation who debuted en masse in the previous window.

One major evolution under Pochettino led to the game’s opening goal. Midway through his tenure, Pochettino cut into Pulisic’s ownership of dead-ball duties, opening the door to alternatives after the Milan winger had too routinely sent his deliveries into the first defender. Malik Tillman made the most of the change, scoring a pair of direct free-kick goals in the World Cup knockout rounds. It also helped Sebastian Berhalter establish himself in a prominent role, transforming from an uncapped outsider when Pochettino arrived into an every-game option capable of filling multiple roles in midfield.

In the ninth minute, Freeman drew a free kick on the right flank roughly 30 yards from goal. Berhalter stood over it as players congregated in the penalty area, curling his delivery around the crowd and beyond the far post. Trusty arrived without a defender in tow, steering the ball back toward the right post for his second international goal.

VAR took some time to confirm that Trusty had stayed onside for such an unobstructed run, and the Celtic defender had plenty to reflect on in the interim. It was his first on-field action in nearly a month, having last played on 15 October following the death of his father, Walt. The decision was met with a series of emphatic claps from Trusty as his teammates returned to celebrate with him for a second time.

Still, Les Grenadiers threatened the US with greater attacking ambition than Mexico or Canada had shown in the previous window. Backed by raucous support, Haiti sustained an intense, swarming press whenever the Americans had possession in their defensive third. In the 16th minute, Danley Jean Jacques fashioned a powerful effort after a quick Haitian break, but Kochen parried the shot away from any would-be follow-up. Lenny Joseph found another opening shortly after the half-hour mark, only for Richards to time his sliding block expertly.

The teams converged near midfield around the 40th minute after an exchange between Adams and Josué Casimir, with the Haiti attacker appearing to attempt to slap Berhalter in the face after the US midfielder intervened on his captain’s behalf. Guatemalan referee Walter López ultimately showed yellow cards to Casimir and Berhalter, and the remainder of the half unfolded in disjointed fashion as neither side looked willing to back down.

The second half sustained that intensity, with both teams leaving a little extra in their challenges. Haiti felt they had earned an attacking free kick in the 52nd minute after Tillman brought down Casimir from behind. As the home-away-from-home faithful booed, the US broke down the flank with a decisive sequence of passes, Pulisic carrying into the final third before slipping the ball left to Robinson.

The left back sent it back into the box for the onrushing Hall, whose movement had afforded him time to pick his spot. The 18-year-old comfortably dispatched his effort into the net. Despite making his debut only in September, Hall already has four goals from five appearances for the US, a tally he looks poised to build on for years to come. Only two other American men have scored four international goals before turning 20: Pulisic and Gio Reyna.

Hall’s appearance on Saturday also officially cap-tied him to the United States, ending any possibility of a one-time switch to Poland, who had courted the teenager.

Hall continued to torment Haiti’s center-backs. Five minutes after his goal, he drew defenders toward him before playing a clever backheel into Pulisic’s path. Carlens Arcus tripped the Milan attacker as he tried in vain to reach the bouncing ball. It was a straightforward penalty decision for López.

Pulisic made no mistake from the spot, opting for power as he drove his effort straight down the middle while goalkeeper Alexandre Pierre dived helplessly away. The American star peeled toward the corner flag for a smiling celebration with a group of young fans before exchanging high-fives with his teammates.…

title: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
author: Kalley Huang
text:
Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman who U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China .

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker , turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding.

“We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

An open letter to Nvidia’s board , titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator.

title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson
author: Jonathan Wilson
text:
Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

M agnusson: And your time starts ... now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in a different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 . Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016 , though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs , and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s .

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director .

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.…
